caption:
Ever been told you've slipped a disc? Here's the thing: discs don't actually slip.

Spinal discs are firmly attached to the bones above and below. They can bulge and irritate nearby nerves, but research suggests many bulges settle over time, and most people improve with time and the right movement.

The word 'slipped' often makes people scared to bend, which can leave backs stiffer. Short walks, gentle movement and gradual strength usually help more.

Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel changes or worsening leg weakness need urgent medical attention. Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios can help you make sense of it. Book online via the link in bio.

Most people do well starting at about half their usual weights and volume for the first week or two, then building up gradually. Mild discomfort during a set is often fine; the next-morning check tells you more. If things are clearly worse 24 hours later, drop back a step.

Overhead press starting to pinch at the top? Lulu bumped up his weight and sets in the same week.

Shoulder pain with overhead lifting usually follows a jump in load, sets or training days rather than one bad rep. Most of the time you don't need to stop training altogether.

caption:
That sharp ache by the dimple in Lulu's lower back? It might involve the sacroiliac joint.

The SI joints link your spine to your pelvis and are built for stability. Despite what you may have heard, they very rarely slip 'out of place'. Pain here is usually about sensitivity and load, and stairs, standing on one leg, rolling over in bed and getting out of the car are common triggers.

Gradual strength work for the glutes, hips and trunk usually helps most. Keeping your knees together getting out of the car can help short term. Fever, leg numbness or weakness, or bladder and bowel changes need prompt medical review.

caption:
The couch is comfy for the first 20 minutes. Then your neck starts talking 🛋️

A laptop on your lap pulls your head down and forward, and soft cushions let your lower back sag. You don't need a full home office to improve things. Raise the screen on a firm cushion or a stack of books, add a cheap wireless keyboard and mouse, and sit into the corner of the couch with a cushion behind your back.

Better still, switch spots through the day: dining table, couch, kitchen bench.

Pain spreading into an arm or leg, building headaches, or stiffness that isn't easing after a week or two are worth an assessment. Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios can help. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Mr Turtle's next massage is a week away, but his back is stiff today. All he needs is a tennis ball and a wall.

One minute on the soles of your feet, one on the calves, one on the glutes, then two minutes on the upper back against a wall, staying off the bony spine. Aim for pressure around 4–6 out of 10 that eases as you go, not builds.

Self-massage won't replace movement or strength work, but it can make both feel a bit easier between appointments. Skip bruises, varicose veins and fresh injuries, and stop if tingling spreads.

caption:
Toto spent half an hour staring at the shoe wall. No shoe will make you injury-proof, but the right one can make running feel a lot better 👟

A good starting point is comfort. Research suggests the shoe that feels comfortable from the first few steps is a sensible pick for most runners. Match it to the running you actually do, and if you're switching to something very different, like much lower drop, mix old and new pairs for a few weeks.
